title: Detection Strategy for Content Injection
summary: This detection strategy covers Content Injection (T1659), where an adversary inserts or alters content inside a network communication so that a user or an automated update process receives something other than what the origin published. The technique matters because it can deliver code or a fake update without ever compromising the origin server, and because the user sees the correct address in the browser while the payload is already changed. Detection depends on network sensor or proxy logs that record response size, content type and hash, transport layer security handshake details such as the certificate issuer, endpoint file records that hash the delivered file, and name resolution logs. It fails most often because legitimate inspection proxies and caching layers also rewrite content.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for content that changes while it travels across the network. The page or file that arrives is not the same as the one that the server sent. Attackers can add code this way without breaking into the server itself.
beginner.whyItMatters: The user sees the right web address, so nothing looks wrong to them. An update file can be replaced in transit and still look normal in the browser. This kind of attack can reach many users at once from one weak point on the path. The evidence is in the difference between the sent content and the delivered content. Catching it protects both the user and the software supply chain.
howItWorks: A network sensor or proxy copies the details of each response, such as its size, type and hash value.
The rule compares that fingerprint with what the origin published or with a known good value.
It also reads the transport security details, because the wrong certificate on the right name is a clue.
On the endpoint, the rule checks the hash of the file that was saved after the download.
Events are joined by user, host, destination name and time to build one delivery story.
A mismatch raises an alert, unless an approved inspection device explains the change.
beginner.example: Think of a sealed medicine box sent by post. The label on the outside is correct, so the pharmacy accepts it. Only when the box is opened does the wrong content appear. Checking the seal is like checking the hash, and the seal is the only thing that proves the contents.
takeaways: Compare what was sent with what arrived, because the address can still look correct.
Certificate details and content hashes are the strongest evidence.
Know which devices in your network are allowed to rewrite traffic.

objectives: Explain how content can be altered in transit without compromising the origin server
Identify network, certificate and endpoint hash telemetry that exposes a mismatch
Document the inspection proxies, caches and content delivery services that legitimately rewrite content
Write a rule that compares the delivered content fingerprint with the expected origin value
Triage a match by confirming the origin hash with the vendor or site owner
Describe the coverage lost when traffic is encrypted and cannot be inspected
dataSources: Network sensor or web proxy logs for hypertext transfer protocol responses recording content type, content length and response hash
Transport layer security handshake records including server name, certificate issuer and negotiated version
Endpoint file creation records with hash values for downloaded files and update packages
Software update client logs showing signature or integrity verification failures
Domain name system query and response logs used to spot unexpected resolution changes for update hosts
logic: The pattern is content delivered to a client that does not match the fingerprint the origin published, or a response that gains an unexpected script element, redirect or file hash on the way. The fields that must be correlated are the requested server name, the certificate issuer and chain, the content type and length, the delivered hash, the requesting user and the process that saved the file. The benign case is an approved inspection proxy, a caching layer that recompresses content, or a captive portal that adds a notice, all of which are known devices with documented behaviour. The malicious case is a hash mismatch on a signed update package, a certificate that does not chain to the expected issuer for that name, or script content added to a response that normally contains only data.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Delivered Content Does Not Match Expected Origin Fingerprint
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: http_response
#     content_type: 'application/octet-stream'
#     hash_mismatch: true
#   filter_inspection:
#     tls_interception: approved
#   condition: selection and not filter_inspection
# level: high
falsePositives: Corporate inspection proxies that decompress and recompress pages before delivering them
Content delivery networks that serve a different but valid build of a file depending on region
Captive portals that insert a login notice into the first page a user requests
Application caching layers that add debugging headers or banners to responses in test environments
tuningNotes: Inventory the devices that are allowed to modify traffic, then filter their addresses and the certificate issuers they use, because those are the main source of noise. Restrict the strictest version of the rule to update and installer downloads for high value software, where a hash mismatch has real consequences, and keep a lower severity version for script content appearing in responses that should carry data only. Baseline the response hashes for the packages your estate downloads most often. The coverage you lose is any injected content inside connections you cannot decrypt, so track encrypted traffic volume per destination and treat uninspected update paths as an accepted risk.
